name: MELAS syndrome
aliases: Mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes

reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / GeneReviews mitochondrial disease
clinicalPearls: The hallmark is recurrent stroke-like episodes producing focal neurological deficits that characteristically do not respect classical vascular territories, often affecting the posterior (parieto-occipital) cortex
The great majority of cases carry the maternally inherited m.3243A>G point mutation in the MT-TL1 gene encoding the mitochondrial transfer RNA for leucine
Expression is governed by heteroplasmy and a tissue threshold effect, so the mutant load, clinical severity and age of onset vary widely within a maternal lineage
Elevated blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate, worsening with exertion, is typical, and MR spectroscopy often shows a lactate doublet within affected cortex
Common systemic features include short stature, sensorineural hearing loss, migraine-like headaches, seizures, diabetes and cardiomyopathy
Muscle biopsy classically shows ragged-red fibres on modified Gomori trichrome staining and strong succinate dehydrogenase but cytochrome c oxidase deficiency in a subset of fibres

Management is supportive, favouring aerobic activity as tolerated, avoidance of mitochondrial toxins, and generic use of cofactor and antioxidant supplements while avoiding agents that impair respiratory-chain function
reference.pathophysiology: MELAS results from a defect of oxidative phosphorylation, most often the m.3243A>G substitution in the mitochondrial transfer RNA(Leu) gene, which impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis and reduces the activity of respiratory-chain complexes. Because mitochondrial DNA is maternally transmitted and present in many copies per cell, a mixture of mutant and normal genomes (heteroplasmy) exists, and disease appears only once the mutant proportion exceeds a tissue-specific threshold. Energy-demanding tissues such as brain, muscle and the endocrine pancreas are preferentially affected. The stroke-like episodes are thought to reflect a combination of neuronal hyperexcitability, an angiopathy of small cerebral vessels with dysfunctional mitochondria in endothelium and smooth muscle, and a mismatch between metabolic demand and impaired energy supply rather than true thromboembolic occlusion.
additionalDifferentials: Ischaemic arterial stroke or cerebral venous thrombosis
Other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies such as MERRF or Leigh syndrome
Complex partial or focal status epilepticus with postictal deficit
CADASIL and other hereditary small-vessel arteriopathies
additionalInvestigations: Resting and post-exercise blood lactate and pyruvate, with cerebrospinal fluid lactate when indicated
Brain MRI showing cortical stroke-like lesions crossing vascular boundaries, plus MR spectroscopy for a lactate peak
Targeted molecular testing for m.3243A>G with heteroplasmy quantification, ideally in urine sediment or muscle rather than blood
Skeletal muscle biopsy for histochemistry (ragged-red fibres) and respiratory-chain enzyme assays
Echocardiography and ECG to screen for cardiomyopathy and conduction disease
Audiometry and fasting glucose to detect associated hearing loss and diabetes
redFlags: Acute stroke-like episode with encephalopathy, seizures or status epilepticus requiring urgent neurological support
New or decompensating cardiomyopathy or cardiac conduction block
Rapidly rising lactic acidosis with metabolic decompensation
Exposure to mitochondrial toxins that may precipitate deterioration
reference.prognosis: MELAS is a progressive multisystem disorder; recurrent stroke-like episodes tend to accumulate neurological disability, dementia and, in many patients, a shortened lifespan, though the course is highly variable and depends on mutant load and organ involvement.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing stroke-like episodes as conventional ischaemic stroke and overlooking the underlying mitochondrial disease
Testing only blood, where the m.3243A>G mutation may be undetectable or at low level; urine or muscle sampling improves yield
Using agents that impair mitochondrial function, which can trigger decompensation
Attributing hearing loss, diabetes or short stature to unrelated causes rather than recognising a unifying maternal disorder
